find: This chapter describes the concepts that have been established and previous studies that have been related that will support Barangayan's design choices. The novelty of the study is the central concept of the study that is presented first together with the formulas, parameters, algorithm and thresholds of Dijkstra routing, and then the central concept of the study that incorporates the Open-Meteo Forecast API and the Historical Weather API rainfall advisory model. The other concepts are implemented in support of the sub-features of the platform. These ideas are found in theory and in literature and Barangayan's design directly addresses these
replacement: This chapter presents the routing model, rainfall advisory, supporting concepts, related studies, and system architecture. The equations define how recorded road conditions affect route cost, while the advisory communicates model-estimated rainfall separately.

find: BARANGAYAN's innovative feature is its evacuation routing module which consists of two modules. The first is Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm which is used to find the safest path for the chosen transportation mode (walking, motorcycle or tricycle, or car) from the resident's phone location to the nearest available Barangay Ampid I evacuation center, along with the paths to the other evacuation centers that are reachable. The second is a rainfall advisory model developed using the Open-Meteo Forecast API and Historical Weather API (Zippenfenig, 2023; Open-Meteo, 2026) which informs the resident, adjacent to the route, of the estimated time of heavy rainfall in the barangay. The Forecast API provides the live advisory and the Historical Weather API was analyzed during development to see the hourly rain of past storms at Ampid I and to choose realistic values for the software tests. Both parts are based on published works, including Dijkstra-based flood evacuation routing (Piamonte et al., 2026; Ogawa et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2022; An et al., 2025; Jeon et al., 2023), rainfall-threshold early warning (Young et al., 2021; Gambini et al., 2024; Dao et al., 2021; Tsai et al., 2022), and Open-Meteo weather data for flood studies and applications (Zhou et al., 2026; Vhajage, 2025; de Lima et al., 2026). The contribution is the integration of flood-weighted routing and a separate rainfall advisory with resident services for Barangay Ampid I. Below are the formulas, parameters, algorithm and thresholds of each part, and how each are utilized in the BARANGAYAN mobile app.
replacement: BARANGAYAN combines Dijkstra evacuation routing with an Open-Meteo rainfall advisory for Barangay Ampid I. Routing selects the available center with the lowest flood-weighted path cost for the chosen transport mode. Published closures, recorded depths, blocked-road marks, and center availability determine the route. Rainfall estimates are displayed separately and do not predict street flooding. The Historical Weather API supports test preparation only. Related routing and warning studies inform this design; the study does not claim worldwide priority or independently established forecast accuracy (Piamonte et al., 2026; Ogawa et al., 2023; Young et al., 2021; Zippenfenig, 2023).

find: D(e) = recorded flood depth of segment e in meters, the typical highest depth that the barangay DRRM has recorded on the street in past floods (D(e) = 0 if no flood is recorded); these values form a historical flood-risk map and are not real-time measurements
replacement: D(e) = the recorded historical depth of segment e, in metres. A measured zero and an unknown value must remain distinct. The current zero fallback for missing records does not establish that a street is dry; routes using it require a visible data limitation.

find: D(e) / Dmax,m, from 0 to 1, using the flood depth DRRM recorded on each street; 0 if no flood is recorded, so the route is then the shortest
replacement: D(e) / Dmax,m for a recorded depth. The current zero fallback for missing data is labelled unknown and is not evidence of a dry road.

find: The novelty of Barangayan is that it combines the safest routes, for walking, motorcycle or tricycle, or car, to the nearest available ECs with the routes to other ECs, and a rainfall advisory from the Open-Meteo Forecast API, whose development used past hourly rainfall from the Historical Weather API, so that each person in Barangay Ampid I gets the safest route to the nearest available EC, the routes to other ECs and a rainfall advisory based on the PAGASA warning bands. The platform aggregates four supporting areas, namely: (1) configurable document services, (2) wide-categorized incident reporting, (3) emergency and disaster risk reduction and management (DRRM) information, and (4) secured digital payment, around this novelty, all designed for Barangay Ampid I. It's powered by a Resident Mobile app created with Expo Router and React Native, an Admin Website created with Next.js, and a shared Supabase backend. That backend is PostgreSQL, authentication, file storage, real-time sync and Edge Functions. This literature review provides affirmation of the direction of the design. It demonstrates that each component part, each evacuation route, each rainfall-threshold warning, each digitized governance, each mobile reporting, each QR payment, each data privacy based on rights are viable and have been proven in published studies some of which are in the Philippines. However, the review cannot determine if the result of the Barangayan system can actually guide residents safely, alert them in time, operate more quickly, be easier to use by residents, staff, or both, or work better in Barangay Ampid I than the systems it is being compared to. The chapters describe the testing and evaluation methods that can help answer those questions.
replacement: The reviewed studies support combining resident services with flood-weighted routing and a separate rainfall advisory. BARANGAYAN applies this design to Ampid I through Android and resident websites, a staff website, and a shared Supabase backend. Its contribution is local integration. Usability, route correctness, geographic accuracy, and service reliability require separate evaluation; findings from other places do not establish performance in Ampid I.
